content: The age-adjusted rates allow for the comparison of geographic areas with differing age structures by standardizing the data to account for variations in age distribution among populations. The table provided, which includes age-adjusted rates, indicates that Fulton County experiences a higher rate of asthma-related emergency room (ER) visits compared to the state of Georgia as a whole. Specifically, Fulton County has a rate of 553.8 per 100,000, whereas the state average is 413.7 per 100,000. By utilizing de-duplicated visits, rates, and age-adjusted rates, one can accurately interpret the data on asthma and home injury hospitalizations and deaths presented later in the report. The data in the table can also be used to calculate a ratio comparing asthma ER visit rates between non-Hispanic Black and non-Hispanic White populations in Georgia and Fulton County. In Georgia, non-Hispanic Black individuals are 3.4 times more likely than non-Hispanic White individuals to visit the ER due to asthma. This ratio was calculated by dividing 783.1 by 227.3. In Fulton County, non-Hispanic Black individuals are 8.4 times more likely than non-Hispanic White individuals to visit the ER due to asthma. This ratio was calculated by dividing 1,048.1 by 124.5. The racial health disparity ratios for asthma hospitalizations and asthma deaths are calculated using the same methodology. A figure illustrating asthma ER visits by age group in Fulton County in 2008 shows that young children aged 0–4 and 5–12 years have higher rates of ER visits for asthma compared to other age groups. In Georgia, non-Hispanic Black individuals are twice as likely as non-Hispanic White individuals to be hospitalized for asthma. In Fulton County, non-Hispanic Black individuals are 4.3 times more likely than non-Hispanic White individuals to be hospitalized for asthma. The age groups with the highest number of asthma-related hospitalizations are individuals aged 45–59 years and 60–74 years. Asthma-related deaths are relatively rare due to preventative care, ongoing treatment, and monitoring. However, because the number of asthma deaths in a single year is small, the data presented spans multiple years (2001–2007) to provide a more comprehensive analysis. There are more asthma-related deaths among White and Black females compared to their male counterparts. This difference may be related to a national trend showing higher asthma prevalence among adult females than adult males. The average number of asthma deaths per year was calculated by dividing the total of 788 deaths by the seven years within the data range. In Georgia, non-Hispanic Black individuals are 2.7 times more likely than non-Hispanic White individuals to die from asthma. In Fulton County, non-Hispanic Black individuals are 3.6 times more likely than non-Hispanic White individuals to die from asthma. In both Georgia and Fulton County, the age-adjusted death rates from asthma are significantly higher for non-Hispanic Black individuals compared to their White counterparts. Nationally, only 32% of households with smokers have adopted smoke-free policies that prohibit smoking inside the home. In Georgia, approximately 63% of middle school students with asthma and 68% of high school students with asthma are exposed to secondhand smoke. Despite the legal age to purchase tobacco products in Georgia being 18 years, a significant number of middle and high school students are cigarette smokers. A notable percentage of adults and high school students with asthma also smoke cigarettes. Ideally, asthma data would be readily available at the national, state, county, Atlanta, and NPU-V levels, collected in a consistent manner to allow for comparisons across geographic areas. Unfortunately, asthma data for Atlanta and NPU-V are not readily available. Instead, asthma prevalence information is often obtained through nationwide interviews, and accurate numbers are not available for smaller geographic areas. The most accessible local data is at the Fulton County level, which can be obtained through the Georgia Department of Community Health's OASIS database. Dr. Matthew Strickland from Emory University has data on asthma ER visits from 41 metro Atlanta hospitals for the years 2002–2004. While the data use agreement prohibits sharing hospital-specific data, aggregate information for all 41 hospitals is available. The data can be sorted by variables such as patient age, sex, race, health insurance, and zip code. The dataset has been processed to exclude same-day repeat visits for the same condition. Dr. Strickland is willing to assist the Center for Working Families in obtaining asthma data for NPU-V zip codes 30310, 30312, and 30315. However, these zip codes cover both NPU-V and neighborhoods south of NPU-V. The asthma information, once sorted by patient zip code, can be further categorized by patient age. Recommended age groupings include 0–4 years (as asthma diagnosis in young children may not be accurate), 5–17 years, 18–59 years, and 60+ years. Unintentional injuries, defined as those occurring without intent to harm, exclude homicide, suicide, and assault. The home, defined as a place where people live independently, excludes dormitories, prisons, nursing homes, long-term care facilities, mental health institutions, shelters, and barracks. The home also includes surrounding areas such as the yard, garage, and driveway. Unintentional home injury encompasses injuries related to the structure of a home (e.g., poor lighting at a staircase leading to falls) and injuries occurring within the home (e.g., accidental medication overdose). Several health indicators for injury are similar to those mentioned in the asthma section, including death records from the National Vital Statistics System, emergency department data from the National Hospital Ambulatory Medical Care Survey, and hospitalization data from the National Hospital Discharge Survey. The National Electronic Injury Surveillance System provides additional data on emergency department visits collected from 100 U.S. hospitals.
